note_on_method: Nobody working on this has played on these courts. Every count, address, price, opening time and lighting statement comes from the City of Scottsdale's own pages — its pickleball page for the counts, addresses and hours, and each park's own page for the cost and the sharing rules. The City lists five locations; four are published here, and the one that is not is named below with the reason. Ashler Hills Park joined this page on 4 September 2026, when this site added a second address resolver — see the last question below.

slots.parking: Scottsdale publishes nothing about parking at any of the four, which is the same gap every city in this directory has. What it does publish instead is more useful than most parking notes would be: the hours, the price, the lighting and the rule for sharing a court when someone is waiting. If you are driving to Horizon Park on a weekday morning — the time the City itself names as busiest — the thing to know is not where to park but that you may be rotating on after a 30-minute game rather than walking straight on. All four are suburban parks in north and east Scottsdale rather than dense street-grid sites, and Ashler Hills is the furthest out, at the northern edge of the city near Cave Creek. None of that is a fact from the City.
slots.peak_hours: This is the first city page in the directory where this section is written from a source rather than from inference. Scottsdale states it, in the same words, on three of the four park pages: "Mornings are typically the busiest time for pickleball play" at Cholla, at Horizon and at Thompson Peak. Twelve cities in, no other operator has published a peak time at all. The City pairs it with the rule that decides what a busy morning actually feels like — play is standard format, first to 11 and win by two, with a 30-minute time limit, "at which time players should rotate off the court with any waiting players". So a queue at 9 a.m. is a queue that moves. Nothing is reservable anywhere in Scottsdale: the City's pickleball page states that courts are first come, first served, that no reservation is required, and that no amplified sound is permitted. Ashler Hills is the exception to none of that except the documentation — its park page names "8 lighted pickleball courts" in the park’s feature list and says nothing else about them, so the rotation rule and the peak-time note are not stated for it.
slots.surface_condition: No surface is stated for any Scottsdale court, which is ordinary — only two cities in this directory have ever published one. What Scottsdale does publish is a piece of maintenance history you can act on: Thompson Peak Park's three courts were closed from 17 August to 11 September 2026 for resurfacing, and were expected to reopen on the 12th, weather permitting. That is a statement about work rather than about a material, so it appears in this city's court notes and not in the surface field. It is also the reason one of the four venues on this page is published as closed rather than as open — the City said so on the day we checked, and a directory that quietly drops that is less useful than one that repeats it.
slots.local_scene: Twenty-nine verified courts across four parks, every one of them lit, and three of the four free to use in the City's own words. Horizon Park's ten courts are the largest single count here; Cholla and Ashler Hills have eight each. What is most striking, though, is not the provision but the documentation: Scottsdale is the only operator we have read that tells you how to behave on a shared court, and the only one that tells you when the courts are busy. The City also runs a free public drop-in programme on Scottsdale Community College's six lighted courts, in partnership with the college — that venue is not published here because the Census places it outside the city limits, but it is real and it is free, and anyone playing in south Scottsdale should know it exists.

best_for.heading: Best if you want the most courts
best_for.text: Horizon Park has ten lighted courts, the largest count in Scottsdale and one of the larger sets anywhere in this directory. Free, drop-in, not reservable, open from sunrise to 10:30 p.m. daily. The City says mornings are typically busiest here, and the sharing rule that applies — 30-minute games, rotate off for anyone waiting — is what makes ten courts feel like ten rather than like four occupied ones.

best_for.heading: Best if you are playing in the evening
best_for.text: Any of them — all four published Scottsdale venues are lit and all four run to 10:30 p.m. Cholla Park is the pick if you want eight courts without Horizon's crowd: the City marks it "Eight outdoor lighted courts", free to use, drop-in and not reservable. In a city where summer daytime play is barely an option, sunrise-to-10:30 p.m. lighting at every venue is the single most valuable thing Scottsdale publishes.

best_for.heading: Best if you do not want to pay
best_for.text: Three of the four state it outright: "They are free to use" appears on the park pages for Cholla, Horizon and Thompson Peak. Across this whole directory only one other city has a verified free court — Portland — and only because Portland wrote the word down too. Ashler Hills is not a paid venue as far as anyone knows; its park page lists the courts among the park’s features and says nothing about cost, so its price is unstated rather than confirmed.

best_for.heading: Best if you are in far north Scottsdale
best_for.text: Ashler Hills Park has eight lighted courts at the northern edge of the city, open sunrise to 10:30 p.m. like every Scottsdale venue. It is the least documented of the four — its park page lists "8 lighted pickleball courts" among the park’s features and stops there, so the price and the rotation rule the City publishes elsewhere are not stated for it — and it is the newest addition to this page, having been unpublishable until this site added a second address resolver in September 2026.

faqs.q: How many pickleball courts does Scottsdale have?
faqs.a: We have verified 29 across four City of Scottsdale venues: ten at Horizon Park, eight each at Cholla Park and Ashler Hills Park, and three at Thompson Peak Park. All are outdoor and all are lit. The City lists a fifth location, Scottsdale Community College, which is not on this page for the reason below.

No, and you cannot. The City's pickleball page states that courts are available on a first come, first served basis and that no reservation is required. It also states that no amplified sound is permitted at any of these locations.

faqs.q: What happens if all the courts are taken?
faqs.a: You wait, and then you play — Scottsdale publishes the rule, which almost no operator does. Court use is limited to standard game format, first side to 11 points or leading by at least two, with a 30-minute time limit, "at which time players should rotate off the court with any waiting players". So the queue moves on a defined clock rather than on whoever is most assertive. That rule appears on the Cholla, Horizon and Thompson Peak park pages; Ashler Hills’ page carries only the count in its feature list, so the rule is not stated there.

Mornings, at the three venues where the City says so: "Mornings are typically the busiest time for pickleball play" appears on the Cholla, Horizon and Thompson Peak pages. This is the only city in this directory whose operator has published a peak time, so it is the only city page here where that answer is a fact rather than an inference.

At three of the four, yes, and the City says so rather than leaving it to be assumed: each of those park pages states "They are free to use". That matters because this directory does not record a court as free unless an operator has written it down. Ashler Hills reads "not verified yet" on cost — not because a charge is suspected, but because its page names the courts and never mentions what they cost.

faqs.q: Why is Thompson Peak Park shown as closed?
faqs.a: Because the City says it is. All three of its pickleball courts were closed from Monday 17 August to Friday 11 September 2026 for resurfacing, and are expected to reopen on Saturday 12 September, weather permitting. This page was checked on 4 September, inside that window. Our build asserts that closure notice is still on the City's page, so when the courts reopen and the notice comes down, the build fails and someone updates this rather than leaving a stale warning.

faqs.q: Why isn't Scottsdale Community College listed?
faqs.a: Because it is not in Scottsdale. The college has six lighted courts that the City runs a free public drop-in programme on in partnership, and the Census geocoder places 9000 E Chaparral Rd in no incorporated place at all — outside the city limits. A city running a programme somewhere does not move that somewhere into the city, so publishing it under Scottsdale would put a venue on a city page it is not in.

faqs.q: Why did Ashler Hills Park only appear recently?
faqs.a: Because our address check could not find it until 4 September 2026. This site requires a street address that resolves before it will publish a venue, and it used one resolver — the US Census address file — which has no record of 32220 N. 74th Way. That day we added a second: OpenStreetMap, consulted only where the Census has nothing, and accepted only when it returns a house number matching the one asked for. It resolves this address, so eight lighted courts that had been refused now publish. The same rule still refuses several other venues whose addresses only resolve to a street, which is the point of setting it at house-number level.

faqs.q: How do you know all this?
faqs.a: From the City of Scottsdale's own pages, snapshotted on 4 September 2026 and committed to the repository that builds this site, so every number here can be checked against the document it came from. The counts, addresses, lighting and hours come from the City's pickleball page; the price and the sharing rules come from each park's own page. Every fact carries its source and the date it was checked.
